Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette: Nia, a 20-year-old African woman and pharmacist in her final year of college, had experienced unspeakable trauma through torture. The event had left an indelible mark on her psyche, shaping not only how she perceived the world but also how she navigated it daily. Nia's torment was so profound that even simple triggers like water or flooding could send her into a panic. This was particularly troubling for her as her hometown in Texas experienced heavy rains and floods during the summer months. The torture had been orchestrated by individuals who systematically stripped her of autonomy, forcing her to do things against her will. These experiences were etched deeply within her, making any situation where she felt pressured or coerced incredibly distressing. At work, this translated into a heightened sensitivity around following strict protocols and procedures that often left her feeling overwhelmed. Nia's boyfriend understood the gravity of what she had been through but sometimes struggled to support her fully without knowing exactly what happened. Arguments, even minor ones, were now potent triggers for her, often spiraling quickly into overwhelming fear and anxiety. Nia found herself avoiding arguments altogether, leading to a growing distance between her and her partner. This avoidance extended to situations where she might be reminded of the event; she would avoid places or people who resembled those involved in the torture. She had come to believe that enduring suffering was part of the aftermath-punishment thinking led her to tell herself she deserved to suffer because of what happened. This belief, though deeply ingrained, was a source of internal conflict and guilt. She felt survivor's remorse for being able to carry on while others did not. Nia's hypervigilance extended into all aspects of her life. Everywhere she went, she meticulously identified escape routes, ensuring she always had an exit strategy in case danger arose again. Her sleep was plagued by nightmares, and she found it difficult to fall asleep without feeling alert-constantly scanning the room for any signs of threat. This hypervigilance meant that even her daily routines were fraught with anxiety. When memories surfaced, Nia's body would reenact the positions and sensations from the traumatic event, leaving her feeling as if she was reliving it in real-time. The fragmented nature of these recollections was disorienting; she felt like only pieces of what happened were accessible to her consciousness. This incompleteness made processing the trauma even more challenging, as she couldn't fully grasp or articulate her experience. Thought avoidance became a survival mechanism for Nia. She had convinced herself that thinking about the event would be too overwhelming to handle, so she actively avoided reflecting on it. However, this strategy only led to increased distress and isolation. Her thoughts were dominated by the need to stay alert, always wary of potential threats. The cumulative effect of these strategies was a life marked by avoidance and hypervigilance. Nia found herself withdrawing from social activities and professional opportunities that once brought her joy. At work, she often felt isolated, struggling to maintain relationships with colleagues due to her heightened sensitivity and need for control over her environment. What finally prompted Nia to seek help was a combination of escalating anxiety and her growing awareness that her relationship might not survive if she did not address these issues. She feared losing the support system she had and hoped therapy could provide her with tools to manage her symptoms, allowing her to reconnect with those around her and regain some semblance of normalcy. In seeking help, Nia expressed a mix of trepidation and hope. The prospect of revisiting such painful memories was daunting, but she was also eager for relief from the constant state of alertness that had become her daily reality. She hoped therapy would offer her not just coping mechanisms but also the chance to integrate her fragmented experiences into a more coherent narrative, thereby restoring some sense of control and peace in her life.
